content:
Today we begin to study the wonderful history of the manna that Yahweh gave to Israel in the wilderness. Israel had come out of Egypt by the mighty hand of Yahweh. They had crossed the Red Sea, but now they were travelling through a dry and difficult land. There were no farms, no shops, and no large supply of food for the whole nation. Yet Yahweh did not leave His people hungry.
He provided food for them every single day throughout their long wilderness journey.

The history of manna begins in Exodus chapter sixteen. Israel had left Egypt and entered the wilderness of Sin. The food they had brought from Egypt was running out, and the people began to complain against Moses and Aaron.
They remembered the food of Egypt and said it would have been better to die there than to come into the wilderness and starve. Their words showed fear and unbelief. They had already seen Yahweh open the Red Sea, yet now they doubted whether He could provide them food. Still, Yahweh heard their complaint and spoke to Moses. He said, "Look, I'm going to rain down food from heaven for you" (Exodus 16:4). God said the people should go out every day and gather only the food they needed for that day. In this way He would test whether they would follow His instructions or not.

God promised to give them meat in the evening and bread in the morning.
That evening, quail came and covered the camp. Then during the night, dew settled around the camp. The next morning, when the dew disappeared, the people saw something unusual upon the ground. Exodus 16:14 says, "When the dew evaporated, a flaky substance as fine as frost blanketed the ground". The people had never seen anything like it before. It was small, fine, and spread across the surface of the wilderness. They looked at one another and asked, "What is it?" (Exodus 16:15). In Hebrew, the expression sounds like **man hu**, meaning, "What is it?" And because they did not know what this strange food was, they called it manna. The name itself came from the very question they asked when they first saw it. Moses then explained that this was the food Yahweh had given them to eat. It was not ordinary food from the earth. It was a special provision from heaven. The people did not create it. They did not plant it. They did not harvest it from any field. God simply gave it to them, fresh, every day.

The Bible gives us several descriptions of what manna looked like. Exodus 16:14 says it was fine and flaky, like frost upon the ground. Exodus 16:31 says, "The manna looked like small coriander seeds, and it was pale yellow like gum resin". Numbers 11:7 compares its appearance to bdellium, a pale, shining resin. From these descriptions, manna appears to have been small, light in colour, and round like a coriander seed, with a pale white or yellowish appearance.

The Bible does not give its exact size, but coriander seeds are small and round, so manna was probably made up of many small flakes or grains spread across the ground. It was fine like frost, but it was not frost. It looked like seed, but it did not grow from the soil. It was a unique food, prepared by Yahweh Himself for His people in the wilderness.

The Bible also tells us what manna tasted like, and it gives us two descriptions. Exodus 16:31 says, "It tasted like honey wafers", showing that manna had a pleasant and sweet taste. Sweet-tasting foods usually contain carbohydrates, especially sugars, which the body breaks down into glucose. Glucose is one of the body’s main sources of energy and helps supply the muscles and brain during physical activity. It can provide quick energy, which would have been useful during a long wilderness journey. Numbers 11:8 gives another description, saying, "It tasted like pastries baked with olive oil". These two descriptions do not contradict one another. The natural manna may have had a sweet taste like honey, and then after it was ground, boiled, or made into cakes, it may have tasted like fresh pastry prepared with oil. Manna was never bitter or unpleasant. Yahweh gave Israel food that was both nourishing and pleasant to eat. And yet, after eating it for a long time, some of the people began to despise it. The problem was never that manna was bad. The problem was that their hearts began to long for the foods of Egypt instead.

There is something tender in the way the manna came. Numbers 11:9 says, "The manna came down on the camp with the dew during the night". The dew settled during the cooler hours of the night. The Bible does not tell us the exact hour, whether it was midnight or early morning. Dew normally forms when the temperature grows cooler in the night, and by early morning the ground around the camp was covered with it. The manna came down together with the dew. Then, when the dew lifted and evaporated, the manna became visible upon the ground. The order seems to have been like this: during the night the dew settled around the camp, the manna came down with the dew, in the morning the dew evaporated, and after the dew disappeared, the manna remained upon the ground, ready for the people to gather. The Manna may have been covered or protected by the dew until the morning light revealed it, lying like fine frost upon the ground.

Yahweh gave clear instructions about how much each person should gather. Exodus 16:16 says, "Pick up two quarts for each person in your tent". The Hebrew measurement was one omer for each person, about two litres by volume, which was enough for one person for one day. Each family gathered according to the number of people living in their tent. A larger family gathered more, and a smaller family gathered less. And here a quiet miracle appeared, for Exodus 16:18 says, "Each family had just what it needed". Those who gathered much did not end up with too much, and those who gathered little did not lack anything. The people also had to gather the manna early in the day, because Exodus 16:21 tells us that when the sun grew hot, the manna melted away. So they could not sleep late and wander out whenever they pleased.

They had to rise early and gather it before the heat of the day. This called for daily attention, daily diligence, and daily obedience. The manna, ground and pounded and boiled and baked, could be prepared in many ways (Numbers 11:8), but it always had to be gathered fresh, in the cool of the morning, by a people who were learning to depend on Yahweh one day at a time.

And here we come to something very strange, something that must have puzzled Israel deeply. Yahweh gave a firm command that on ordinary days, no one was to keep any manna until the next morning. Not a handful was to be stored away. Yet one day of every week that rule would be completely reversed, and the manna kept overnight would remain perfectly fresh. Why would the same food that rotted on one day stay good on another? Why would Yahweh forbid them to store it, and then, on a certain day, command them to do the very thing He had forbidden? There was a deep lesson hidden inside this daily bread; a lesson about rest, about trust, and about a holy day set apart by Yahweh Himself. That is where we will continue tomorrow.

title: Prayer
text:
O Father, our God,

We thank You that in a dry and empty land, You rained down bread from heaven.

You did not leave Your people to starve, but fed them faithfully every single morning.

Teach us to depend on You one day at a time, as Israel depended on the manna.

Help us to rise and gather what You provide, and never to despise Your daily gifts.

You know exactly what each of us needs, and You give us neither too much nor too little.

"You gave them bread from heaven when they were hungry." - Nehemiah 9:15

In the name of Christ, the true bread from heaven, we pray. Amen.
